strengths: Addresses an important question about what multimodal contrastive learning recovers, using an intuitive model that separates coupled latent variables from modality-specific information.

The proposed PCA/FastICA postprocessing is simple and reuses frozen CLIP models. Experiments cover multiple encoders and datasets, with useful reported gains: ViT-B/16 two-shot target-domain average accuracy increases from 32.51% to 37.13%.

Synthetic experiments examine several distributional and geometric assumption violations and report variability over three runs. CelebA traversals provide suggestive qualitative examples of interpretable directions.
weaknesses: The central proof contains a fundamental error. Appendix D.1, Lemma 5.1 asserts that the normalized contrastive loss has global minimum zero and requires exact alignment of paired representations. Under the stated finite-concentration vMF model, the latent joint distribution has full support, so exact pairwise alignment would force constant representations, contradicting the required uniformity. Moreover, the correctly matched density-ratio solution achieves normalized loss -2I(z_x;z_t)<0. Both Theorems 4.1 and 4.3 rely on this invalid lemma, leaving the central identifiability guarantees unestablished.

The convex-body proof has an additional substantive problem: Equation (43) treats p(z_t) as exactly uniform, whereas Lemma 4.2 only asserts convergence as lambda approaches zero. A normalized distance kernel on a bounded convex body generally produces a nonuniform marginal at finite lambda because of boundary effects. Corollary 4.4 also omits the restriction to non-Euclidean L-alpha metrics that its appendix proof requires.

The theoretical justification for FastICA in Section 5 is incompatible with the uniform hyperspherical prior. Its coordinates are dependent and its distribution is rotationally invariant, so ICA cannot identify a distinguished component basis. Having M-1 intrinsic dimensions does not resolve this issue. The proposed local-isometry/PCA connection to the convex-body result is also heuristic rather than a demonstrated guarantee.

The downstream experiments do not isolate disentanglement from whitening and dimensionality reduction. Appendix K uses different reduced dimensions, but matched PCA-only and whitening-only controls are absent. An orthogonal ICA rotation after fixed whitening preserves dot products and the optimized L2-regularized linear-probe objective, making these controls essential before attributing the gains to independent components.

The empirical recovery evidence is insufficient. Appendix K computes R2 by predicting learned representations from true latents; this can be perfect for a rank-deficient linear projection that discards latent information. Reverse prediction and rank checks are needed to establish recovery. Selected CelebA traversals and downstream accuracy improvements also do not establish real-data identifiability, and quantitative disentanglement comparisons are missing.

The causal contribution is overstated. The undirected edge specifies observational dependence without establishing interventional semantics or identifying the underlying causal relationship. Much of the geometric identifiability argument reuses Zimmermann et al. [67], placing substantial weight on the multimodal bridge whose proof is invalid.

Reproducibility and statistical evaluation remain incomplete: the samples used to fit PCA/FastICA and the component-count selection protocol are unclear, real-data results lack repeated-split uncertainty estimates, and synthetic training configurations are underspecified. These omissions limit confidence in the few-shot comparisons.
